concept.name: Consumer-Driven Contract Testing

relationships.description: Connects Consumer-Driven Contract Testing to contract testing in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: A testing methodology where API consumers publish executable expectations (contracts) that providers verify in isolation, catching breaking schema or behavioral changes in CI without slow shared staging environments.
spark.keyTakeaway: Replace brittle end-to-end staging suites with Pact V4 contracts and `can-i-deploy` matrix checks so every microservice can deploy independently in under 60 seconds.

concept.whyItMatters: In distributed microservice architectures, a single unannounced field rename or status-code shift breaks downstream consumers in production. Shared staging E2E environments become flaky bottlenecks that slow releases to a crawl while still missing edge-case consumer assumptions.
whenToUse: Polyglot microservice teams deploying dozens of services independently on different release cadences.
Internal REST, GraphQL, or event-driven (Kafka/RabbitMQ) APIs with clearly identifiable internal consumers.
Replacing slow, flaky multi-service integration tests in shared QA/staging environments.
whenNotToUse: Public third-party APIs with thousands of unknown external consumers (use OpenAPI/Protobuf schema-first contracts instead).
Monolithic applications where all modules compile and test together in a single binary.
Testing deep business logic, database migrations, or multi-step UI workflows—contracts only test the boundary.
keyPoints: In Consumer-Driven Contract Testing (CDCT), the consumer defines *only* the fields, headers, and status codes it actually uses—giving providers freedom to evolve unused fields.
Consumers run unit tests against a local mock server (e.g., Pact Mock Service) that records interactions into a declarative JSON contract file.
Contracts are published to a central **Pact Broker** (or PactFlow) tagged with Git branch, SHA, and deployment environment.
Providers replay every active consumer's contract against their real HTTP handler or message consumer using **Provider States** (`given(...)`) to seed deterministic fixtures.
The `can-i-deploy` CLI queries the Broker's verification matrix in CI/CD, acting as a zero-staging deployment gate.

examples.title: Preventing a Silent Checkout Outage
examples.scenario: The `orders-api` team planned to refactor `total_cents` (integer) to `totalAmount` (object) across 12 endpoints, assuming only `checkout-web` consumed it.
examples.outcome: Running Pact provider verification against the Pact Broker immediately failed on the `invoices-worker` consumer contract, revealing an undocumented dependency on `total_cents` in 6 seconds during PR CI.

examples.title: Async Kafka Event Contracts for Inventory
examples.scenario: An `inventory-svc` published `StockReserved` Avro/JSON events to Kafka, and 4 downstream consumers kept breaking when optional fields became nullable.
examples.outcome: Adopting Pact V4 Message Pacts verified serialization/deserialization handlers in both producer and consumer CIs without spinning up Kafka or Zookeeper containers.

tradeOffs.pro: CDCT proves which fields consumers *actually* read and catches behavioral/status-code mismatches.
tradeOffs.con: Requires cross-team coordination to maintain a Pact Broker and write Provider State setup hooks.

tradeOffs.factor: Strict Matchers vs. Flexible Type Matchers
tradeOffs.pro: Using `like()`, `eachLike()`, and regex matchers avoids brittle tests tied to hardcoded timestamps or UUIDs.
tradeOffs.con: Overly loose matchers (`like("string")`) can miss domain format regressions such as ISO-8601 date format changes.

tradeOffs.factor: Isolated Verification vs. Full Staging E2E
tradeOffs.pro: Runs in 5–15 seconds per service with zero network flakiness and 100% deterministic fixtures.
tradeOffs.con: Does not validate infrastructure wiring (IAM, Kubernetes Ingress, mTLS, or real database query performance).

failureModes.name: Stale Provider States
failureModes.description: A provider state hook (`given('user 42 has active cart')`) seeds mock data that drifts from actual database constraints, passing tests while failing in prod.
failureModes.mitigation: Execute provider state setup against real in-memory/Testcontainers repositories rather than stubbing out the entire service layer.

failureModes.name: Over-Specified Exact Matchers
failureModes.description: Consumers assert exact literal strings (`"2026-11-12T10:00:00Z"`) or exact array lengths, blocking harmless provider updates.
failureModes.mitigation: Use Pact type/regex matchers (`iso8601DateTime()`, `eachLike()`) and assert only the fields the consumer deserializes.

failureModes.name: Missing `can-i-deploy` Gate
failureModes.description: Teams publish and verify pacts in CI but never run `can-i-deploy` before deploying, allowing unverified consumer versions into production.
failureModes.mitigation: Make `pact-broker can-i-deploy --pacticipant ... --to-environment prod` a mandatory blocking step in CD pipelines.

failureModes.name: Contract-as-Unit-Test Anti-Pattern
failureModes.description: Consumers write 40 pact interactions testing every validation rule and business edge case, turning contracts into slow duplicate unit suites.
failureModes.mitigation: Limit contracts to boundary shapes: 1 happy path + key error schemas (400/404/409/503) per endpoint.

commonMistakes: Testing the consumer's mock client rather than its real HTTP/gRPC serialization layer.
Forgetting to call `record-deployment` in the Pact Broker after a service ships, leaving `can-i-deploy` blind to what is live in production.
Including non-consumer-used fields in the contract expectation, unnecessarily coupling provider evolution.
Using CDCT for public external APIs where you cannot ask external developers to run Pact tests.
Stubbing out the provider's own JSON serializer during verification, which defeats the purpose of checking wire compatibility.

sections.content:
## The idea

Traditional integration testing demands that Service A and Service B run simultaneously in a shared environment. As microservices scale beyond 10–15 services, keeping all versions synchronized in staging becomes quadratically expensive and chronically flaky. **Consumer-Driven Contract Testing (CDCT)** inverts this dependency: instead of testing live services together, each **consumer** writes fast unit tests against a local mock that records its exact HTTP or message expectations into a **contract** (a Pact file).

That contract is published to a **Pact Broker**, where the **provider** downloads it and replays every interaction against its real controller/serializer in complete isolation. Because the consumer only specifies the fields and status codes it actually reads, the provider gains full visibility into which parts of its API are safe to refactor—and the Broker's verification matrix answers *"Is it safe to deploy Service X to production right now?"* in under two seconds.

## Concrete walkthrough

Follow a change between `checkout-web` (Consumer) and `orders-api` (Provider):

1. **Consumer Test**: `checkout-web` runs Jest with `@pact-foundation/pact`. It declares an interaction: `given("order ORD-99 is PENDING")`, `POST /v2/orders/ORD-99/confirm` expecting `200 OK` with `{ "orderId": string, "status": "CONFIRMED" }`. The Pact mock server validates `checkout-web`'s real Axios client and writes `checkout-web-orders-api.json`.
2. **Publish**: CI runs `pact-broker publish --consumer-app-version $GIT_SHA --branch main`, triggering a webhook to `orders-api`.
3. **Provider Verification**: `orders-api` pulls the contract, boots its FastAPI/Spring Boot app with a Testcontainers Postgres instance, executes the `order ORD-99 is PENDING` state handler to insert a row, and replays the `POST` request.
4. **Matrix Gate**: Before `orders-api` deploys, CD runs `pact-broker can-i-deploy --pacticipant orders-api --version $GIT_SHA --to-environment prod`. Only if all live consumer versions in `prod` are verified green does the rollout proceed.

data.caption: CDCT decouples consumer and provider release cycles through a central verification matrix rather than synchronized staging deployments.

sections.content:
## Bi-directional contracts and async messaging

Pure CDCT works best for internal teams who own both ends of an API. When providers already maintain strict **OpenAPI 3.1** or **Protobuf** schemas—or serve external consumers—**Bi-Directional Contract Testing** (supported by PactFlow and `oasdiff`) bridges the gap: the provider uploads its OpenAPI spec verified by its own tests, the consumer uploads its Pact expectations, and the Broker mathematically checks that the consumer contract is a valid subset of the provider's schema.

For event-driven architectures (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SNS/SQS), **Pact V4 Asynchronous Message** contracts replace HTTP request/response pairs with `{ metadata, contents }` assertions. The consumer verifies its Kafka deserializer against the sample payload, while the provider verifies that its domain event publisher emits matching JSON/Avro payloads.

## Contract testing approaches compared

| Approach | Best For | Runtime Speed | Catches Behavioral Mismatches? | Adoption Overhead |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Pact (CDCT)** | Internal REST/GraphQL/Kafka microservices | 5–15s per service | Yes (status codes, headers, state) | Medium (Broker + Provider States) |
| **Bi-Directional (OpenAPI + Pact)** | Teams with mature OpenAPI/Swagger specs | <5s (schema comparison) | Partial (schema subset only) | Low (no Provider State hooks) |
| **Protobuf / Buf Breaking** | gRPC & strongly typed internal meshes | <2s | No (wire types & field IDs only) | Very Low (linter in PR CI) |
| **Shared Staging E2E** | Final smoke check & infra/IAM wiring | 15–60 min | Yes, but slow & flaky | High (environment maintenance) |

## Failure modes

The most frequent organizational failure is **forgetting `record-deployment`**: without knowing which SHA is currently running in `staging` or `prod`, `can-i-deploy` either checks nothing or blocks against dead feature branches. Technically, **mocked provider state handlers** create a false sense of security—if the state handler bypasses real serialization or database constraints, a passing Pact run can still 500 in production. Finally, **exact-value assertions** on timestamps, UUIDs, or array ordering turn contracts brittle and cause constant cross-team friction.

## Rollout strategy for existing platforms

Never attempt a big-bang migration across 50 services. Start with your highest-churn consumer-provider pair (usually the API gateway/BFF and its primary core domain service). Enable Pact in **work-in-progress (`pending`)** mode first so newly added consumer expectations do not immediately block the provider's main branch until the provider implements them. Once `can-i-deploy` is wired into both pipelines and running reliably for two weeks, expand to asynchronous Kafka/SQS boundaries and decommission redundant staging E2E tests.

## Practical checklist

- Use **Pact V4** type/regex matchers (`like`, `eachLike`, `iso8601DateTime`) instead of hardcoded literal values.
- Test the consumer's **real HTTP/Kafka client**, never a hand-rolled stub.
- Implement **Provider State** hooks against real serialization and Testcontainers/in-memory stores.
- Enable `pendingPacts` and `includeWipPactsSince` so new consumer features don't break provider `main` prematurely.
- Gate every production deploy with `pact-broker can-i-deploy` and follow every rollout with `record-deployment`.
- Restrict contracts to boundary shapes and error codes—keep business-rule permutations in fast unit tests.

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Contract Testing Consumer Driven

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: A testing methodology where API consumers publish executable expectations (contracts) that providers verify in isolation, catching breaking schema or behavioral changes in CI without slow shared staging environments.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Provider CI applies the primary invariant and coordinates with CD Deployment Gate.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, CD Deployment Gate experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Execute provider state setup against real in-memory/Testcontainers repositories rather than stubbing out the entire service layer.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Replace brittle end-to-end staging suites with Pact V4 contracts and `can-i-deploy` matrix checks so every microservice can deploy independently in under 60 seconds.
Avoid trap: Testing the consumer's mock client rather than its real HTTP/gRPC serialization layer.
Avoid trap: Forgetting to call `record-deployment` in the Pact Broker after a service ships, leaving `can-i-deploy` blind to what is live in production.
When to reach for it: Polyglot microservice teams deploying dozens of services independently on different release cadences.
When to reach for it: Internal REST, GraphQL, or event-driven (Kafka/RabbitMQ) APIs with clearly identifiable internal consumers.

putItTogether.title: Putting Contract Testing Consumer Driven Together
putItTogether.summary: Replace brittle end-to-end staging suites with Pact V4 contracts and `can-i-deploy` matrix checks so every microservice can deploy independently in under 60 seconds.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Contract Testing Consumer Driven before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Running Pact provider verification against the Pact Broker immediately failed on the `invoices-worker` consumer contract, revealing an undocumented dependency on `total_cents` in 6 seconds during PR CI.
